newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan toughens press law ahead of elections.
newsitem.headline: Jordan toughens press law ahead of elections.

text.p: King Hussein has unveiled a tough new press law setting sweeping restrictions on reporting, and stiffening fines for offenders ahead of Jordan's parliamentary elections later this year.

A royal decree issued late on Saturday, just days after the king lashed out at the "deteriorating morals" of journalists, also imposed crushing financial obligations on Jordan's opposition-dominated weekly newspapers.

The government has "ensured that the journalistic freedom will be a responsible freedom at the service of the country and its people," Information Minister Samir Mutawae told the state Petra news agency.

The revised law expands the "10 Commandments", a central article of the press law listing 10 areas off limits to journalists, to include an 11th catch-all ban on subjects "which include false information or rumours which lead to harming the general interest or government institutions or its workers".

It forbids journalists outright from writing about Jordan's armed forces and security services and retains a ban on anything which offends the king and royal family, contains contempt of religion, damages national unity, encourages crime, undermines confidence in the Jordanian dinar or offends public morals.

The prohibitions cover drawings and pictures as well as written articles. Fines for violators were raised to at least 15,000 dinars ($21,200) from 1,000 dinars. Offending newspapers can be suspended from publication.
Journalists vowed in a statement on Sunday to oppose the law which they said aimed at gagging opposition before elections due in November.
They said they would consider a legal appeal against the law, issued in temporary form while parliament is in recess.
The opposition Islamic Action Front slammed it as a "massacre of the press and assassination of democracy".

Under the law weekly newspapers, often boisterous critics of King Hussein's 1994 peace treaty with Israel, have been given just three months to increase their capital 20-fold to 300,000 dinars from 15,000 dinars.
Journalists said the new financial requirements would force many of Jordan's 30 or so weeklies, most of which have a circulation of just a few thousand, to fold.
The decree for the first time prevents non-Jordanians from editing newspapers. Authorities have often accused opposition papers of being mouthpieces for foreigners undermining national stability.
It also cancels a pledge to cut the state's 61 percent controlling take in Jordan's top-selling newspaper, Al-Rai, to just 30 percent.
"The press is not reflecting the correct image about the country which we know," King Hussein told senior army officers in a speech last week. "This distortion should stop."

He said Jordan's press was suffering from "deteriorating morals", citing criticism of democracy in Jordan and what he said were untrue stories that he donated $300,000 to families of Israeli schoolgirls shot dead by a Jordanian soldier.
Dozens of Jordanian journalists already face charges for their writings. Some of them, tried under penal law instead of the press law, have received prison terms of up to nine months.
